```{python}
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap, to_hex

shade = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("shade", ["#bfe0b0", "#ffffff", "#f5b8cb"])


def scoreboard(table, rules=None, by="column", decimals=3, size="0.75em", padding="3px"):
    """A results table in Great Tables: green is better, pink is worse, the best in bold."""
    df = table.to_frame() if isinstance(table, pd.Series) else table.copy()
    df.index = [str(i) for i in df.index]
    df.columns = [str(c) for c in df.columns]
    rules = rules or {c: "lower" for c in df.columns}
    gt = (GT(df.reset_index(names="row"), rowname_col="row")
          .fmt_number(columns=list(df.select_dtypes("number").columns), decimals=decimals)
          .sub_missing(missing_text="")
          .tab_options(table_font_size=size, data_row_padding=padding))
    for c, rule in rules.items():
        values = df[c].astype(float)
        bad = values if rule == "lower" else -values if rule == "higher" else (values - rule).abs()
        lo, hi = np.nanmin(bad), np.nanmax(bad)
        for i, b in enumerate(bad):
            if np.isnan(b):
                continue
            fill = to_hex(shade((b - lo) / (hi - lo) if hi > lo else 0.0))
            look = [gt_style.fill(color=fill)] + ([gt_style.text(weight="bold")] if b == np.nanmin(bad) else [])
            gt = gt.tab_style(style=look, locations=loc.body(columns=c, rows=[i]))
    return gt


def box(ax, x, y, w, h, text, colour, size=13):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, y), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02", facecolor="white",
                                edgecolor=colour, linewidth=2))
    ax.text(x + w / 2, y + h / 2, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=size)


def arrow(ax, x0, y0, x1, y1, colour="grey"):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, y1), xytext=(x0, y0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=colour, lw=1.5))


# The case of the book from chapter 3 on: weekly sales of four Walmart stores
walmart = pd.read_csv("../data/walmart.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
walmart = (walmart[walmart["unique_id"].isin([1, 2, 3, 4])]
           .sort_values(["unique_id", "ds"]).reset_index(drop=True))
H, WINDOWS = 8, 4
dates = np.sort(walmart["ds"].unique())
cutoffs = [dates[len(dates) - (WINDOWS - k) * H - 1] for k in range(WINDOWS)]


def windows():
    """The book's protocol: four windows of eight weeks; each model sees only the weeks before."""
    for cutoff in cutoffs:
        history = walmart[walmart["ds"] <= cutoff]
        window = walmart[walmart["ds"] > cutoff].groupby("unique_id").head(H)
        yield cutoff, history, window


def contexts(history):
    return [torch.tensor(g["y"].to_numpy(), dtype=torch.float32) for _, g in history.groupby("unique_id")]


cv = {}          # model name -> DataFrame of unique_id, ds, prediction over the four windows
seconds = {}     # model name -> inference time over the four windows


def record(name, frames, start):
    cv[name] = pd.concat(frames)[["unique_id", "ds", name]]
    seconds[name] = time.time() - start


def smape(y, f):
    return float(np.mean(200 * np.abs(y - f) / (np.abs(y) + np.abs(f))))
```

# Where this fits

## The last step away from "one series" {.smaller}

| Week | Models | Trained on | At forecast time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–8 | ETS, ARIMA, regression, Prophet | **your series** | fit, then forecast |
| 9 | NNAR, NeuralProphet | your series | fit, then forecast |
| 9 | LightGBM, N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TFT | **your dataset** | fit, then forecast |
| **10** | **TimeGPT, Chronos, Moirai, TimesFM** | **millions of other series** | **forecast only** |

Week 9's verdict: on M3, ten neural architectures trained on 1428 series, untuned, did not beat ETS
and Theta. Today's models were trained on hundreds of thousands of series, by teams with clusters of
GPUs — and you use them **without training anything**.

The question has not changed: **does it beat the benchmark on a holdout it never saw?** — and, more
than ever, *how do we know it never saw it?*

## The book this lecture follows {.smaller}

reference for this week. We take its steps in its order:

2. **Building a tiny foundation model** yourself.

6. **Moirai** — any number of variables.

# Understanding foundation models

## Algorithm, model, foundation model {.smaller}

An **algorithm** is the recipe; the **data** are the ingredients; the **model** is the cake. Least
squares is an algorithm; *your* regression line is a model. The same recipe on different data gives a
different model.

A **foundation model** (Stanford HAI, 2021) is a model trained on **large, diverse data** so that it can
be applied to **many tasks**. Peixeiro's four marks of one:

| | What it means for forecasting |
|---|---|
| **large, diverse training data** | billions of observations, every frequency and domain |
| **a large model** | tens of millions to hundreds of millions of weights |
| **many tasks** | any series, any frequency, any horizon — without retraining |
| **adaptable** | can be **fine-tuned**: a few more training steps on your data |

Almost all of them are **transformers** — so before any of them, what a transformer does with a series.

## A transformer, from a time series' point of view {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: transformer
#| fig-align: center

            connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.25"))
ax.text(9.0, -0.07, "each prediction is fed back to the decoder (autoregression)", color=red_pink, ha="center", fontsize=9)
```

**Tokens** — single values or **patches**; **embedding** — each token as a long vector; **encoder** —
how tokens relate; **decoder** — the forecast, piece by piece, each fed back in. Many models keep only
one half: that choice is most of the difference between them.

## Positional encoding: telling the model *when* {.smaller}

Attention by itself sees a **set** of tokens, not a sequence: shuffle them and it cannot tell. So each
position $p$ gets a fixed vector added to its embedding:

$$
PE_{(p,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \qquad
PE_{(p,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)
$$

```{python}
#| label: positional
#| fig-align: center
positions, d = 64, 64
p = np.arange(positions)[:, None]
i = np.arange(d // 2)[None, :]
pe = np.zeros((positions, d))
pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(p / 10000 ** (2 * i / d))
pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(p / 10000 ** (2 * i / d))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 2.9), width_ratios=[1.3, 1])
axes[0].imshow(pe.T, aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu_r")
axes[0].set_xlabel("position in the series")
axes[0].set_ylabel("embedding dimension")
axes[0].set_title("The positional-encoding matrix")
for dim, colour in zip([0, 6, 20], [red_pink, blue, turquoise]):
    axes[1].plot(pe[:, dim], color=colour, label=f"dimension {dim}")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("Clock hands at different speeds")
plt.show()
```

Peixeiro's image: **clock hands**. Each dimension turns at its own speed; read together they give the
exact position — as hour, minute and second hands give the exact time.

## Self-attention: which past matters {.smaller}

Each token asks a **query** $q$, every token offers a **key** $k$ and a **value** $v$; the output is
a weighted average of values, weighted by how well query and key match:

$$
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right) V
$$

```{python}
#| label: attention
#| fig-align: center
co2 = pd.read_csv("../data/co2_mauna_loa.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
recent = co2[co2["ds"] >= "2015-01-01"].reset_index(drop=True)
values = recent["y"].to_numpy()
tokens = np.array([values[t - 11:t + 1] - values[t - 11:t + 1].mean() for t in range(11, len(values))])
tokens = tokens / tokens.std(axis=1, keepdims=True)
query = tokens[-1]
scores = tokens[:-1] @ query / np.sqrt(tokens.shape[1])
weights = np.exp(scores - scores.max())
weights /= weights.sum()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.8))
lag = np.arange(len(weights), 0, -1)
ax.bar(lag, weights, color=[red_pink if l % 12 == 0 else "lightgray" for l in lag], width=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("how many months back the token is")
ax.set_ylabel("attention weight")
ax.invert_xaxis()
ax.set_title("The latest 12-month window of CO₂ attends to its own months in earlier years (lags 12, 24, 36, … in pink)")
plt.show()
```

No weights were trained here: each token is a 12-month stretch of CO₂, and $q \cdot k$ is their
similarity. Even so, attention finds the season by itself. A trained model learns **projections** for
$Q, K, V$, and runs many such **heads** in parallel — one may track the trend, another the season.

## Five models, three shapes {.smaller}

| Model | From | Transformer part | Tokens | Output | Covariates |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TimeGPT** | Nixtla | encoder + decoder | values | point + conformal interval | yes |
| **Lag-Llama** | academic | decoder only | lags + calendar features | Student-$t$ distribution | no |
| **Chronos** | Amazon | encoder + decoder (T5) | binned values | distribution over 4096 bins | Chronos-2: yes |
| **Moirai** | Salesforce | encoder only | patches | mixture of distributions | yes |
| **TimesFM** | Google | decoder only | patches | point (+ quantiles) | yes |

: {tbl-colwidths="[13,11,17,19,24,16]"}

**Pros**, as Peixeiro lists them: forecasting out of the box; good with few data points; less expertise
needed; one model for many tasks. **Cons**: privacy (some run on someone else's server); no control over
what the model can do; not best for every case; heavy — gigabytes of weights, a GPU for speed.

# Building a tiny foundation model

## Pretrain, transfer, fine-tune — at home {.smaller}

Peixeiro's chapter 2 builds a foundation model in miniature, to make three words concrete:

- **Pretraining:** train once on many series.
- **Transfer learning:** apply the trained model to a series it has **never seen**. With no further
  training, that is **zero-shot** forecasting.
- **Fine-tuning:** a few more training steps on the new series, starting from the pretrained weights.

Our pretraining corpus: all 1428 **M3 Monthly** series from Week 9. The model: **N-BEATS**, 12 months
ahead from 24 months of input.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast
from neuralforecast.models import NBEATS

quiet = dict(enable_progress_bar=False, logger=False, enable_model_summary=False)
m3 = pd.read_csv("../data/m3_monthly.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
pretrained = NeuralForecast(
    models=[NBEATS(h=12, input_size=24, max_steps=1000, scaler_type="robust", random_seed=1, **quiet)],
    freq="MS")
pretrained.fit(m3)                      # about a minute on a laptop CPU
```

`scaler_type="robust"` is our one change to the book's code: without scaling, the network fitted on
M3's scales is thrown by CO₂'s ~400 ppm, and a single fine-tuning step moved its forecast by 100 ppm.

## Zero-shot, fine-tuned, trained from scratch {.smaller}

The new series: **CO₂ at Mauna Loa** (Week 8's practice), monthly since 2005 — not in M3. Last 12 months
held out.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
import copy

co2_df = co2[co2["ds"] >= "2005-01-01"].assign(unique_id="co2")[["unique_id", "ds", "y"]]
co2_train, co2_test = co2_df.iloc[:-12], co2_df.iloc[-12:]

zero_shot = pretrained.predict(df=co2_train)                     # never trained on CO₂

fine_tuned = copy.deepcopy(pretrained)
fine_tuned.models[0].trainer_kwargs["max_steps"] = 10            # ten more steps, on CO₂ only
fine_tuned.fit(co2_train)

from_scratch = NeuralForecast(
    models=[NBEATS(h=12, input_size=24, max_steps=100, scaler_type="robust", random_seed=1, **quiet)],
    freq="MS")
from_scratch.fit(co2_train)
```

```{python}
#| include: false
tiny = {"zero-shot (pretrained on M3)": zero_shot["NBEATS"].to_numpy(),
        "fine-tuned, 10 steps": fine_tuned.predict()["NBEATS"].to_numpy(),
        "trained on CO₂ only": from_scratch.predict()["NBEATS"].to_numpy(),
        "seasonal naive": co2_train["y"].to_numpy()[-12:]}
co2_y = co2_test["y"].to_numpy()
tiny_table = pd.DataFrame({name: {"MAE": np.mean(np.abs(co2_y - f)), "sMAPE, %": smape(co2_y, f)}
                           for name, f in tiny.items()}).T
```

**Zero-shot works** — a third of seasonal naive's error on a series the model never saw. Ten fine-tuning
steps change nothing. A network trained on CO₂ alone is **better still**: twenty regular years are enough.
The book found the pretrained model first on its series; the order depends on what the new series can teach.

## Another frequency {.smaller}

The book's second test: the model pretrained on **monthly** data, asked about **daily** data. Ours:
Melbourne's daily maximum temperature, 2012–2014 (`vic_elec`, Week 7), 12 days ahead, over **ten
windows** — one 12-day window of weather is mostly noise.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
vic = pd.read_csv("../data/vic_elec.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
daily = (vic[vic["unique_id"] == "Temperature"].set_index("ds")["y"].resample("D").max()
         .reset_index().assign(unique_id="temp")[["unique_id", "ds", "y"]])
start = len(daily) - 10 * 12
daily_errors = {"zero-shot (monthly model)": [], "naive": []}
for k in range(10):
    history = daily.iloc[:start + 12 * k]
    actual = daily["y"].iloc[start + 12 * k:start + 12 * (k + 1)].to_numpy()
    daily_errors["zero-shot (monthly model)"].append(
        np.mean(np.abs(actual - pretrained.predict(df=history)["NBEATS"].to_numpy())))
    daily_errors["naive"].append(np.mean(np.abs(actual - history["y"].iloc[-1])))

daily_model = NeuralForecast(
    models=[NBEATS(h=12, input_size=24, max_steps=500, scaler_type="robust", random_seed=1, **quiet)],
    freq="D")
daily_cv = daily_model.cross_validation(df=daily, n_windows=10, step_size=12, refit=False)
daily_errors["trained on the daily series"] = [np.mean(np.abs(g["y"] - g["NBEATS"]))
                                               for _, g in daily_cv.groupby("cutoff")]
```

## The monthly model on daily data {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: tiny-daily
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.0))
for (name, errs), colour in zip(daily_errors.items(), [red_pink, slate, blue]):
    ax.plot(range(1, 11), errs, "o-", color=colour, label=f"{name}: mean MAE {np.mean(errs):.2f} °C")
ax.set_xlabel("window")
ax.set_ylabel("MAE, °C")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

In the book, the monthly model failed on daily data. **Ours did not**: over ten windows it beat both
the naive forecast and a network trained on the daily series itself. Twelve days of weather are mostly
noise around a level, and a robustly scaled N-BEATS forecasts a level well whatever frequency it learned
on. One experiment is not a law — the book's or ours. That is the point of scoring every claim.

## What a real foundation model needs {.smaller}

What our miniature could not do, and every model that follows was built to fix:

- **One horizon.** It forecasts exactly 12 steps — the `h` it was trained with. A real one must take any
  horizon: 7 days or 168 hours. Solved by **generating** the output step by step (TimeGPT, Chronos) or
  in long **output patches** (TimesFM).
- **One frequency, one domain.** Trained on M3's monthly series only. Real corpora mix every frequency
  from seconds to years and domains from electricity to web traffic — billions of observations.
- **Data.** Text is everywhere; public time series are scarce. That is why the teams build their own
  corpora, mix series together and generate synthetic ones — and why they rarely say exactly what is in
  them.
- **Compute.** Our pretraining took a minute on a laptop. Chronos-T5 (Large) took 18 hours on eight
  A100 GPUs.

# TimeGPT

## A generative pretrained transformer for time series {.smaller}

**TimeGPT** (Garza et al., 2023; Nixtla) was the first foundation model for forecasting — and the only
one here you cannot download.

- A full **encoder–decoder** transformer. **Generative**: the decoder produces the forecast one step at a
  time, feeding each back in, so the horizon can be any length.
- It estimates the conditional distribution of the future given the past **and covariates**:
  $$P\left(y_{t+1:t+h} \mid y_{0:t},\, x_{0:t+h}\right) = f_\theta\left(y_{0:t},\, x_{0:t+h}\right)$$
  The covariates $x$ are needed **up to $t + h$**: their future must be known, or forecast first.
- Trained on about **100 billion** observations from finance, health, energy, web and more — the
  sources are not disclosed. Kept raw: noise and outliers included.

## Intervals by conformal prediction {.smaller}

TimeGPT's intervals do not come from a distribution in the model. They come from its **errors on the
past** — Week 8's conformal intervals:

```{python}
#| label: conformal
#| fig-align: center
actual = np.array([[8, 4, 5], [7, 5, 6]])
predicted = np.array([[6, 7, 4], [8.5, 2.5, 5.2]])
scores = np.abs(actual - predicted).ravel()                 # conformity scores, all windows
forecast = np.array([6.0, 7.0, 8.0])
candidates = forecast[:, None] + np.concatenate([scores, -scores])[None, :]
lo, hi = np.percentile(candidates, [10, 90], axis=1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.7))
for step in range(3):
    ax.scatter(np.full(candidates.shape[1], step + 1), candidates[step], color="lightgray", s=40, zorder=2)
ax.fill_between([1, 2, 3], lo, hi, color=red_pink, alpha=0.2, label="80% interval: 10th–90th percentile")
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], forecast, "o-", color=red_pink, label="point forecast")
ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 3], ["h = 1", "h = 2", "h = 3"])
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
ax.set_title(f"The book's example: errors {np.round(scores, 1).tolist()} from two past windows")
plt.show()
```

1. Forecast past windows, where the answer is known (cross-validation); keep the absolute errors.
2. Add and subtract every error to the new point forecast: a cloud of possible values.
3. The 80% interval is its 10th to 90th percentile — here **3.55 to 8.45** around the first forecast of 6.

## Access: an API key {.smaller}

TimeGPT runs on Nixtla's servers: your notebook sends the data and receives the forecast.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
from nixtla import NixtlaClient

client = NixtlaClient()                 # reads NIXTLA_API_KEY from the environment
client.validate_api_key()

forecast = client.forecast(df=history, h=8, freq="W-FRI", level=[80],
                           time_col="ds", target_col="y", id_col="unique_id")
```

- **The key:** sign in at [dashboard.nixtla.io](https://dashboard.nixtla.io) with Google or GitHub,
  *API Keys* → *Create*. Step by step, with Colab secrets: the **TimeGPT setup handout** on Moodle.
- **The trial:** 30 days, free, no card; then access ends unless the account is paid for. Create the
  key when you need it — for the final project — not before.
- **The data leaves your machine.** Fine for public data; ask first for an employer's.

The TimeGPT numbers in this lecture were computed once by `infra/timegpt_walmart.py` and are read from a
file, so rendering the slides spends no calls.

## The case: four Walmart stores {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: walmart
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8), sharex=True)
for ax, (store, g) in zip(axes.ravel(), walmart.groupby("unique_id")):
    ax.plot(g["ds"], g["y"] / 1e6, color=slate, linewidth=1)
    holidays = g[g["holiday"] == 1]
    ax.scatter(holidays["ds"], holidays["y"] / 1e6, color=red_pink, s=14, zorder=3)
    ax.axvspan(cutoffs[0], g["ds"].max(), color=orange, alpha=0.08)
    ax.set_title(f"Store {store}", fontsize=10)
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("$ million / week")
fig.suptitle("Weekly sales, Feb 2010 – Oct 2012; pink: holiday weeks; shaded: the 32 weeks of the four test windows",
             fontsize=11)
plt.show()
```

**The protocol, for every model from here on:** the last 32 weeks cut into **four windows of 8 weeks**;
for each window the model sees only the weeks before it. Scored by MAE and sMAPE, as in the book. The
one covariate is the **holiday flag** — the only one whose future is genuinely known.

```{python}
#| include: false
from pathlib import Path
HAVE_TIMEGPT = Path("../data/fm_timegpt_walmart.csv").exists()
if HAVE_TIMEGPT:
    timegpt = pd.read_csv("../data/fm_timegpt_walmart.csv", parse_dates=["ds", "cutoff"])
    for name in ["TimeGPT", "TimeGPT fine-tuned", "TimeGPT fine-tuned, depth 2", "TimeGPT + holiday"]:
        cv[name] = timegpt[["unique_id", "ds", name]]
    timing = pd.read_csv("../data/fm_timegpt_timing.csv", index_col=0)["seconds"]
    seconds.update(timing.to_dict())
```

## TimeGPT, zero-shot {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: timegpt-zero
#| fig-align: center
if HAVE_TIMEGPT:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 4.0), sharex=True)
    for ax, (store, g) in zip(axes.ravel(), timegpt.groupby("unique_id")):
        hist = walmart[(walmart["unique_id"] == store) & (walmart["ds"] > dates[-60])]
        ax.plot(hist["ds"], hist["y"] / 1e6, color=slate, linewidth=1)
        for cutoff, w in g.groupby("cutoff"):
            ax.fill_between(w["ds"], w["TimeGPT-lo-80"] / 1e6, w["TimeGPT-hi-80"] / 1e6, color=red_pink, alpha=0.18)
            ax.plot(w["ds"], w["TimeGPT"] / 1e6, color=red_pink, linewidth=1.6)
        ax.set_title(f"Store {store}", fontsize=10)
    fig.suptitle("Four windows, each forecast from the weeks before it; band: 80% conformal interval", fontsize=11)
    plt.show()
else:
    print("Run infra/timegpt_walmart.py to fetch the TimeGPT forecasts.")
```

Each window's forecast follows the store's level and its weekly swings; the four 80% bands differ in
width from store to store and window to window — each built from that store's past errors. Over the
32 weeks TimeGPT's sMAPE is about 3.1%, on the same level as Chronos-2's.

## Fine-tuning TimeGPT {.smaller}

Fine-tuning is a request parameter: the server trains a copy of the model on your series for a few
steps, then forecasts.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
client.cross_validation(df=history, h=8, n_windows=4, step_size=8, freq="W-FRI",
                        finetune_steps=10,          # gradient steps on your data
                        finetune_loss="mae",        # what those steps minimise
                        finetune_depth=2)           # 1 = only the last layers ... 5 = all of them
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAVE_TIMEGPT:
    variants = ["TimeGPT", "TimeGPT fine-tuned", "TimeGPT fine-tuned, depth 2", "TimeGPT + holiday"]
    display(scoreboard(pd.DataFrame({v: {"MAE": np.mean(np.abs(timegpt["y"] - timegpt[v])),
                                         "sMAPE, %": smape(timegpt["y"], timegpt[v]),
                                         "seconds": seconds.get(v, np.nan)}
                                     for v in variants}).T, decimals=2))
```

- Ten fine-tuning steps improve the MAE by about 1% — less than the 6% the book reports on its data.
- **Depth 2 gives exactly the same forecasts as depth 1** here. The documentation does not say what each
  depth tunes; on four short series, more of the model had nothing more to learn.
- The holiday flag helps a little more than fine-tuning, and costs nothing extra.

## What the holiday flag contributes {.smaller}

With covariates, TimeGPT can return **Shapley values**: how much each covariate moved each forecast.

```{python}
#| label: timegpt-shap
#| fig-align: center
if HAVE_TIMEGPT:
    shap = pd.read_csv("../data/fm_timegpt_shap.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.8))
    for store, g in shap.groupby("unique_id"):
        ax.plot(g["ds"], g["holiday"] / 1e3, "o-", label=f"Store {store}")
    ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_ylabel("$ thousand")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=4)
    ax.set_title("Shapley value of the holiday flag in each forecast week of the last window")
    plt.show()
```

The last window has one holiday week per store — Labor Day. The flag's Shapley value is no larger that
week than on ordinary weeks, and its sign changes from week to week. A Shapley value describes how the
**model** responds to an input, not the effect of a holiday on sales; with one holiday in the window
there is little for either to show.

## Anomalies, by the same machinery {.smaller}

TimeGPT has no separate anomaly model. It forecasts every past week from the weeks before it with a
**99% interval**; a week outside its interval is flagged.

```{python}
#| label: timegpt-anomalies
#| fig-align: center
if HAVE_TIMEGPT:
    anomalies = pd.read_csv("../data/fm_timegpt_anomalies.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.0), sharey=False)
    for ax, store in zip(axes, [1, 2]):
        g = anomalies[anomalies["unique_id"] == store]
        ax.plot(walmart.loc[walmart["unique_id"] == store, "ds"], walmart.loc[walmart["unique_id"] == store, "y"] / 1e6,
                color=slate, linewidth=1)
        ax.fill_between(g["ds"], g["TimeGPT-lo-99"] / 1e6, g["TimeGPT-hi-99"] / 1e6, color=turquoise, alpha=0.2)
        flagged = g[g["anomaly"].astype(bool)]
        ax.scatter(flagged["ds"], flagged["y"] / 1e6, color=red_pink, s=30, zorder=3)
        ax.set_title(f"Store {store}: {len(flagged)} weeks flagged", fontsize=10)
    plt.show()
```

- The nine flagged weeks are **Black Friday and the week before Christmas 2011** in all four stores, and
  Easter 2012 in one. They are the year's predictable peaks — outside the interval because the
  interval was built from ordinary weeks. "Anomalous" means *surprising to the model*, not to the store.
- The first year is the context for the first forecast, so it cannot be checked. The client's default
  model flagged *every* week here; `model="timegpt-1"`, the book's, works — check before you trust.

# Lag-Llama

## Open, probabilistic, decoder-only {.smaller}

**Lag-Llama** (Rasul et al., 2024) borrows Meta's **LLaMA** language model — decoder only — and changes
what a token is:

- A token for time $t$ holds **lagged values** $y_{t-1}, y_{t-7}, y_{t-12}, \dots$ from a fixed context,
  plus **calendar features** at every scale: second-of-minute up to quarter-of-year. Which of them
  change from step to step tells the model the frequency.
- The output is not a number but the three parameters of a **Student-$t$** distribution — mean, scale,
  degrees of freedom — so every forecast comes with its spread (Week 9's DeepAR, pretrained).
- Pretrained on 20 datasets — energy, transport, nature, air quality — at **daily, hourly, 15-minute and
  1-minute** frequencies only, on horizons of 24 to 60 steps.

That last line is a warning: it has **never seen weekly or monthly data**. Chapter 2's experiment
predicts what follows. Peixeiro recommends fine-tuning it before use outside its frequencies.

In practice it is a research repository, not a package: you clone it and work inside it. The book's
current code no longer uses it; neither do we.

# Chronos

## A language model that reads a time series {.smaller}

**Chronos** (Ansari et al., 2024; Amazon) changes nothing in the language model. It changes the series,
so that an off-the-shelf **T5** can read it:

```{python}
#| label: chronos-tokens
#| fig-align: center
store1 = walmart[walmart["unique_id"] == 1]["y"].to_numpy()
scaled = store1 / np.mean(np.abs(store1))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 2.8))
axes[0].plot(store1 / 1e6, color=slate)
axes[0].set_title("Store 1, $ million")
for ax, bins, colour in zip(axes[1:], [100, 5], [blue, red_pink]):
    edges = np.linspace(scaled.min(), scaled.max(), bins + 1)
    token = np.clip(np.digitize(scaled, edges) - 1, 0, bins - 1)
    ax.step(range(len(token)), token, where="mid", color=colour)
    ax.set_title(f"Mean-scaled, then {bins} bins: the tokens", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```

1. **Mean scaling:** divide by the mean absolute value — millions of dollars and dozens of cars on one
   scale.
2. **Quantisation:** clip to $[-15, 15]$ and cut into **4094 equal bins**. Each value becomes a bin
   number: a word from a vocabulary. With 5 bins (right) the series says almost nothing.
3. Train the T5 to predict the next token with **cross-entropy** — regression done as classification.
   Forecasting is sampling tokens; many samples give the quantiles.

## Where the data came from {.smaller}

Public time series are scarce, so Chronos made more of them:

```{python}
#| label: augmentation
#| fig-align: center
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
sales = store1[:100] / np.mean(np.abs(store1[:100]))
traffic_ = vic[vic["unique_id"] == "Demand"]["y"].to_numpy()[:100 * 48:48]
traffic_ = traffic_ / np.mean(np.abs(traffic_))
lam = 0.6
t = np.arange(100)
kernel_trend, kernel_season = 0.01 * t, 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 2.8))
axes[0].plot(sales, color="lightgray", label="Walmart store 1")
axes[0].plot(traffic_, color="silver", linestyle="--", label="Victoria electricity")
axes[0].plot(lam * sales + (1 - lam) * traffic_, color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="TSMixup, λ = 0.6")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_title("TSMixup: a convex mix of real series")
axes[1].plot(kernel_trend, color="lightgray", label="linear kernel")
axes[1].plot(kernel_season, color="silver", linestyle="--", label="periodic kernel")
axes[1].plot(kernel_trend + kernel_season + rng.normal(0, 0.08, 100), color=blue, linewidth=1.8,
             label="sum, with noise")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("KernelSynth: random kernels, combined")
plt.show()
```

- **TSMixup:** scale random series from different domains and take a weighted average — new series with
  the shapes of several.
- **KernelSynth:** sample basic patterns — trend, periodic, noise — and add or multiply them: a million
  synthetic series.
- With these, 28 real datasets — about **890,000 series, 84 billion observations** — became 10 million
  training series.

## The Chronos family {.smaller}

| Model | Parameters | Pretraining | What changed |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Chronos-T5 tiny … large | 8M … 710M | up to 18 h on 8 A100 GPUs ($2,066) | the original: tokens, sampled one at a time |
| **Chronos-Bolt** small | 48M | | reads **patches**, outputs all quantiles at once: up to 250× faster |
| **Chronos-2** | 120M | | **group attention**: several series and **covariates** in one forecast |

The book's warning about binning: the model has a bin for the largest value it has seen, and **no token
for a new record**. On a strong trend with a short context its forecasts tend to flatten.

## Chronos on the four stores {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from chronos import BaseChronosPipeline

bolt = BaseChronosPipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-bolt-small", device_map="cpu")
chronos2 = BaseChronosPipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-2", device_map="cpu")

for name, pipe in [("Chronos-Bolt", bolt), ("Chronos-2", chronos2)]:
    start, frames = time.time(), []
    for cutoff, history, window in windows():
        _, mean = pipe.predict_quantiles(contexts(history), prediction_length=H, quantile_levels=[0.5])
        frames.append(window.assign(**{name: np.concatenate([np.asarray(m).ravel() for m in mean])}))
    record(name, frames, start)

start, frames = time.time(), []                       # Chronos-2 with the holiday flag as a known covariate
for cutoff, history, window in windows():
    out = chronos2.predict_df(history[["unique_id", "ds", "y", "holiday"]],
                              future_df=window[["unique_id", "ds", "holiday"]],
                              id_column="unique_id", timestamp_column="ds", target="y",
                              prediction_length=H, quantile_levels=[0.5])
    frames.append(window.merge(out.rename(columns={"predictions": "Chronos-2 + holiday"}),
                               on=["unique_id", "ds"]))
record("Chronos-2 + holiday", frames, start)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
truth = walmart[["unique_id", "ds", "y"]]


def score(names):
    rows = {}
    for name in names:
        merged = truth.merge(cv[name], on=["unique_id", "ds"])
        rows[name] = {"MAE": np.mean(np.abs(merged["y"] - merged[name])),
                      "sMAPE, %": smape(merged["y"], merged[name]),
                      "seconds": seconds.get(name, np.nan)}
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).T


scoreboard(score(["Chronos-Bolt", "Chronos-2", "Chronos-2 + holiday"]), decimals=2)
```

## Fine-tuning Chronos-2 {.smaller}

Since version 2 the package fine-tunes on a laptop:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
import tempfile

first_history = walmart[walmart["ds"] <= cutoffs[0]]            # only the weeks before all four windows
tuned = chronos2.fit(contexts(first_history), prediction_length=H, num_steps=50, batch_size=32,
                     learning_rate=1e-5, output_dir=tempfile.mkdtemp(), remove_printer_callback=True,
                     disable_tqdm=True, report_to="none")

start, frames = time.time(), []
for cutoff, history, window in windows():
    _, mean = tuned.predict_quantiles(contexts(history), prediction_length=H, quantile_levels=[0.5])
    frames.append(window.assign(**{"Chronos-2 fine-tuned": np.concatenate([np.asarray(m).ravel() for m in mean])}))
record("Chronos-2 fine-tuned", frames, start)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
scoreboard(score(["Chronos-2", "Chronos-2 fine-tuned"]), decimals=2)
```

Fifty steps on the weeks before the first window move the score in the second decimal. The learning
rate is small on purpose: fine-tuning should adjust a pretrained model, not overwrite it. Like every
other choice, it is a candidate to be scored, not an improvement to be assumed.

## A covariate that matters more {.smaller}

The holiday flag is one week in a few. A bigger test of covariates — Week 8's **Messi page views**, the
2026 World Cup. Chronos-2 was released in October 2025: it **cannot have seen** this.

```{python}
#| label: world-cup
#| fig-align: center
messi = pd.read_csv("../data/messi_wikipedia.csv", parse_dates=["ds"]).assign(item_id="messi")
messi["y"] = np.log(messi["y"])
tournaments = [("2016-06-03", 23), ("2018-06-14", 31), ("2019-06-14", 23), ("2021-06-13", 27),
               ("2022-11-20", 28), ("2024-06-20", 24), ("2026-06-11", 38)]
messi["tournament"] = 0
for begin, days in tournaments:
    messi.loc[messi["ds"].between(begin, pd.Timestamp(begin) + pd.Timedelta(days=days)), "tournament"] = 1
history_wc = messi[messi["ds"] < "2026-06-11"]
future_wc = messi[messi["ds"] >= "2026-06-11"].head(51)
settings = dict(id_column="item_id", timestamp_column="ds", target="y", prediction_length=51,
                quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
alone = chronos2.predict_df(history_wc[["item_id", "ds", "y"]], **settings)
with_flag = chronos2.predict_df(history_wc[["item_id", "ds", "y", "tournament"]],
                                future_df=future_wc[["item_id", "ds", "tournament"]], **settings)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.0))
recent_m = messi[messi["ds"].between("2026-04-01", future_wc["ds"].max())]
ax.plot(recent_m["ds"], recent_m["y"], color=slate, linewidth=1.2, label="actual")
ax.plot(future_wc["ds"], alone["predictions"], color=blue, linewidth=1.8, label="Chronos-2, history only")
ax.plot(future_wc["ds"], with_flag["predictions"], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="Chronos-2 + tournament flag")
ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp("2026-06-11"), pd.Timestamp("2026-07-19"), color=orange, alpha=0.08)
ax.set_ylabel("log views")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
wc_y = future_wc["y"].to_numpy()
print(f"MAE on log views: history only {np.mean(np.abs(wc_y - alone['predictions'])):.2f}, "
      f"with the flag {np.mean(np.abs(wc_y - with_flag['predictions'])):.2f}")
```

The flag lifts the forecast for the tournament and brings it down after the final — learned from the
six earlier tournaments in the context, with nothing fitted. It still falls far short of the peaks.

# Moirai

## Built for any number of variables {.smaller}

**Moirai** (Woo et al., 2024; Salesforce) — an **encoder-only** transformer with three ideas:

```{python}
#| label: moirai-ideas
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.2))
x = np.linspace(-4, 8, 400)
comp = {"Student-t": 0.5 * stats.t.pdf(x, df=3, loc=0, scale=1), "log-normal": 0.5 * stats.lognorm.pdf(x, s=0.5, scale=2.5)}
for (name, dens), colour in zip(comp.items(), ["silver", "lightgray"]):
    axes[0].plot(x, dens, color=colour, linestyle="--", label=f"{name}, weight 0.5")
axes[0].plot(x, sum(comp.values()), color=red_pink, linewidth=2, label="the mixture")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_title("A mixture of distributions: asymmetric if it needs to be")
series = {"target": walmart[walmart["unique_id"] == 1]["y"].to_numpy()[:16] / 1e6,
          "holiday": walmart[walmart["unique_id"] == 1]["holiday"].to_numpy()[:16] * 0.3 + 1.2}
pos = 0
for (name, v), colour in zip(series.items(), [blue, orange]):
    for patch in range(4):
        axes[1].plot(range(pos + 4 * patch, pos + 4 * patch + 4), v[4 * patch:4 * patch + 4], color=colour, linewidth=2)
        axes[1].axvspan(pos + 4 * patch, pos + 4 * patch + 3.8, color=colour, alpha=0.06)
    axes[1].text(pos + 8, 2.0, name, color=colour, ha="center")
    pos += 17
axes[1].set_yticks([])
axes[1].set_title("Any-variate: every variable patched and laid end to end")
plt.show()
```

- **Patches** whose length depends on the frequency: 8 for yearly data, 16–32 for weekly, 32–128 for
  per-minute. One embedding layer per patch size.
- **Any-variate attention:** the target and every covariate are flattened into **one long sequence**; a
  learned bias tells attention whether two patches come from the same variable or from different ones.
  Add a covariate and the sequence just gets longer.
- A **mixture** of Student-$t$, log-normal, negative binomial and a low-variance normal as output.

## LOTSA, and what came after {.smaller}

Moirai's team published its corpus: **LOTSA**, 27 billion observations from nine domains — the largest
open collection at the time.

| Frequency | Datasets | Observations |
|---|---:|---:|
| yearly, quarterly | 9 | 3.2 million |
| monthly, weekly | 17 | 29.5 million |
| daily | 21 | 709 million |
| hourly | 31 | 19.9 billion |
| minute, second | 27 | 7.0 billion |

72% of it is hourly; yearly series are 0.003%. Training therefore **caps** each dataset's share, so the
model does not become an hourly specialist.

**Moirai-MoE** (2024) switches to a decoder with a **mixture of experts** — several feed-forward networks,
a gate picking two per token. **Moirai 2.0** (2025) is the current version.

## Moirai on the four stores {.smaller}

`uni2ts`, Moirai's package, needs older `numpy` and `pandas` than this course, so it runs in its own
environment (`infra/moirai_walmart.py`); the deck reads its forecasts.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
from uni2ts.model.moirai import MoiraiForecast, MoiraiModule

model = MoiraiForecast(module=MoiraiModule.from_pretrained("Salesforce/moirai-1.1-R-small"),
                       prediction_length=8, context_length=128, patch_size="auto", num_samples=200,
                       target_dim=1, feat_dynamic_real_dim=1, past_feat_dynamic_real_dim=0)
forecasts = model.create_predictor(batch_size=32).predict(dataset)   # a GluonTS dataset
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
moirai = pd.read_csv("../data/fm_moirai_walmart.csv", parse_dates=["ds", "cutoff"])
for name in ["Moirai", "Moirai + holiday", "Moirai-2.0"]:
    cv[name] = moirai[["unique_id", "ds", name]]
seconds.update(pd.read_csv("../data/fm_moirai_timing.csv", index_col=0)["seconds"].to_dict())
scoreboard(score(["Moirai", "Moirai + holiday", "Moirai-2.0"]), decimals=2)
```

Moirai-1.1 small is the weakest foundation model on this case; the holiday flag helps it more than any
other model here, and the newer Moirai 2.0 beats both. The book's capstone found the same — Moirai
small among the weakest — and pointed to the size: it is the smallest model of its family.

# TimesFM

## A point forecaster with long output patches {.smaller}

**TimesFM** (Das et al., 2024; Google) is **decoder-only** and, unlike the others, trained for a **point
forecast** — mean squared error, not a distribution.

```{python}
#| label: timesfm-patches
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.3))
for k in range(4):
    box(ax, k * 1.05, 0.3, 1.0, 0.4, f"input patch\n32 values", blue, 11)
box(ax, 4.5, 0.3, 1.4, 0.4, "decoder", red_pink, 12)
box(ax, 6.4, 0.3, 4.2, 0.4, "output patch: 128 values at once", orange, 12)
arrow(ax, 4.2, 0.5, 4.5, 0.5)
arrow(ax, 5.9, 0.5, 6.4, 0.5)
ax.text(5.3, 0.05, "256 steps ahead = 2 passes, not 8", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=slate)
ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 10.8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.8)
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
```

- Input **patches of 32**, output **patches of 128**: long horizons need few autoregressive passes, so
  errors compound less. Random masking during training makes any context length work.
- Pretrained on about **380 billion** observations — and roughly **98% of them are Wikipedia page
  views**, plus Google Trends, M4 and synthetic series.

That corpus has a consequence for Week 8's Messi example: Wikipedia page views up to the model's
training date may well be **in** it. A zero-shot score on page views says less about TimesFM than about
any other model here.

## TimesFM on the four stores {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
import timesfm

tfm = timesfm.TimesFM_2p5_200M_torch.from_pretrained("google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch")
tfm.compile(timesfm.ForecastConfig(max_context=512, max_horizon=128, normalize_inputs=True,
                                   use_continuous_quantile_head=True, return_backcast=True))

for name in ["TimesFM", "TimesFM + holiday"]:
    start, frames = time.time(), []
    for cutoff, history, window in windows():
        inputs = [c.numpy() for c in contexts(history)]
        if name == "TimesFM":
            point, _ = tfm.forecast(horizon=H, inputs=inputs)
            point = [p[-H:] for p in np.asarray(point)]
        else:          # flag over context + horizon; a linear "xreg" step: pip install "timesfm[xreg]"
            flags = [np.concatenate([h["holiday"], w["holiday"]]).tolist() for (_, h), (_, w)
                     in zip(history.groupby("unique_id"), window.groupby("unique_id"))]
            point, _ = tfm.forecast_with_covariates(inputs=[i.tolist() for i in inputs],
                                                    dynamic_numerical_covariates={"holiday": flags})
            point = [np.asarray(p)[-H:] for p in point]
        frames.append(window.assign(**{name: np.concatenate(point)}))
    record(name, frames, start)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
scoreboard(score(["TimesFM", "TimesFM + holiday"]), decimals=2)
```


# Language models as forecasters

## Forecasting as a question {.smaller}

Peixeiro's chapter 8 asks plain LLMs — Flan-T5, Llama-3.2 — for a forecast, in words. The recipe:
**scale** the series, show one **worked example** (few-shot), ask, then **parse** numbers out of the text.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
import re
from transformers import AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM, AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google/flan-t5-base")
flan = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained("google/flan-t5-base")

history1 = walmart[(walmart["unique_id"] == 1) & (walmart["ds"] <= cutoffs[-1])]["y"].to_numpy()
low, high = history1.min(), history1.max()
scale = lambda v: (v - low) / (high - low)
text = lambda v: ", ".join(f"{x:.3f}" for x in v)
prompt = (f"Input: The last 16 scaled values of weekly sales were {text(scale(history1[-32:-16]))}. "
          f"What will be the next 8 values?\nOutput: {text(scale(history1[-16:-8]))}\n"
          f"Input: The last 16 scaled values of weekly sales were {text(scale(history1[-16:]))}. "
          f"What will be the next 8 values?\nOutput:")
answer = tokenizer.decode(flan.generate(tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids,
                                        max_new_tokens=80, do_sample=False)[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
numbers = [float(x) for x in re.findall(r"-?\d+\.\d+|-?\d+", answer)][:H]
llm_forecast = np.array((numbers + [numbers[-1]] * H)[:H]) * (high - low) + low
actual1 = walmart[(walmart["unique_id"] == 1)]["y"].to_numpy()[-H:]
print(f"The model answered: '{answer}'  ({len(numbers)} numbers for 8 weeks)")
print(f"sMAPE: Flan-T5 {smape(actual1, llm_forecast):.2f}%,  "
      f"seasonal naive {smape(actual1, history1[-52:-52 + H]):.2f}%  — store 1, last window")
```

## Time-LLM, and what language models add {.smaller}

**Time-LLM** (Jin et al., 2024; chapter 9) keeps a frozen LLM and learns a translation into it:

- **Patch reprogramming:** each patch of the series is mapped onto a small set of learned **text
  prototypes** — combinations of the LLM's word embeddings that come to mean "short up, then steady
  down".
- **Prompt-as-prefix:** a text description of the data and the task is put in front of the patches.
- It has **no zero-shot mode**: the translation layer must be trained on your data every time. It is in
  `neuralforecast` as `TimeLLM`.

Peixeiro's verdict across chapters 8–10: asking an LLM in words works, roughly, and loses to the models
built for time series; Time-LLM does better than plain prompting, at the cost of training. Our one
window above says the same: a language model answers a question about numbers with **words** — here,
fewer than were asked for.

# The capstone

## Every model, one protocol {.smaller}

The book's chapter 10 ends with a model comparison on data no model could have seen. Ours: the four
stores, four windows of 8 weeks, with **the benchmarks of this course** alongside — they are what the
book's comparison does not include.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
for model in [SeasonalNaive(season_length=52, alias="seasonal naive"),
              AutoETS(season_length=1, alias="ETS"),          # weekly: m = 52 is beyond ETS
              AutoARIMA(season_length=52, alias="ARIMA")]:
    start, frames = time.time(), []
    for cutoff, history, window in windows():
        local = StatsForecast(models=[model], freq="W-FRI")
        frames.append(window.merge(local.forecast(df=history[["unique_id", "ds", "y"]], h=H),
                                   on=["unique_id", "ds"]))
    record(model.alias, frames, start)

import tirex
tirex_model = tirex.load_model("NX-AI/TiRex", device="cpu")      # xLSTM-based, 35M parameters, 2025
start, frames = time.time(), []
for cutoff, history, window in windows():
    _, mean = tirex_model.forecast(context=contexts(history), prediction_length=H)
    frames.append(window.assign(TiRex=np.asarray(mean).ravel()))
record("TiRex", frames, start)
```

## Accuracy against time {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: accuracy-time

local_names = {"seasonal naive", "ETS", "ARIMA"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.2))
for name, row in board.iterrows():
    colour = slate if name in local_names else (orange if name.startswith("TimeGPT") else red_pink)
    ax.scatter(max(row["seconds"], 0.05), row["sMAPE, %"], s=60, color=colour, zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(name, (max(row["seconds"], 0.05), row["sMAPE, %"]), xytext=(5, 3), textcoords="offset points",
                fontsize=8)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("seconds for all four windows (log scale; TimeGPT includes the network round trip)")
```

## What the scoreboard says {.smaller}

- **The top five are all foundation models**, Chronos-2 with the holiday flag first. TimeGPT, Chronos-2 and
  TimesFM are within a few tenths of a point of each other.
- **ARIMA is the best of this course's models** — ahead of TiRex, Chronos-Bolt and every Moirai. ETS, with
  no weekly season to model, and seasonal naive are last.
- **Most open models forecast four stores × four windows in a few seconds or less on a CPU** — less than
  ARIMA's search over orders. Timings move from run to run; TimeGPT's are mostly the network round trip.
- **Four series, 128 forecasts.** A difference of a tenth of a point is within noise here. What the board
  shows is the band each model falls in, not a ranking to trust to the decimal.

# Did it see the answer?

## Leakage, tested {.smaller}

A zero-shot score is only zero-shot if the test data were not in the pretraining corpus. **M4 Monthly**
is in the corpora of Chronos and Chronos-2, with each series' last 18 months held out; **M3** is in
neither. If a model **remembers**, it should do unusually well on the M4 months it saw.

```{python}
#| echo: false
leak = pd.read_csv("../data/foundation_leakage.csv")       # built by infra/foundation_leakage.py


def memory_effect(df, model):
    r = np.log(df[model] / df["ETS"]).groupby([df["dataset"], df["window"]]).mean()
    return np.exp((r["M4", "pretraining window"] - r["M4", "held-out test"])
                  - (r["M3", "pretraining window"] - r["M3", "held-out test"]))


def resample(df, rng):
    parts = []
    for _, d in df.groupby("dataset"):
        ids = d["unique_id"].unique()
        parts.append(d.set_index("unique_id").loc[rng.choice(ids, len(ids))].reset_index())
    return pd.concat(parts)


rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
rows = {}
for model in ["Chronos-Bolt", "Chronos-2", "snaive"]:
    boot = [memory_effect(resample(leak, rng), model) for _ in range(300)]
    rows[model] = {"memory effect": memory_effect(leak, model),
                   "2.5%": np.percentile(boot, 2.5), "97.5%": np.percentile(boot, 97.5)}
scoreboard(pd.DataFrame(rows).T, rules={"memory effect": 1.0})
```

- 1000 series from each set, two windows each, MASE relative to ETS. Below 1 would mean "better on what
  it saw". **Both Chronos models sit at 1**: no memory of the windows they were trained on.
- The seasonal-naive row is a **placebo**: it moves (1.14) because the windows differ — so the test can
  see a difference when there is one.
- What this does not show: that the corpus never matters. If your **holdout itself** were in it, nothing
  but the release date would protect you.

## A zero-shot comparison you can trust {.smaller}

The final project asks for one — 2 points, for the setup, not for who wins:

1. **Same cutoff, same horizon, same metric** as your own model. The foundation model gets the training
   history as context and nothing after it.
2. **No choosing on the test set.** Picking the best of five foundation models by their test score is
   selection on the test — Week 3's oldest mistake. Choose on validation windows.
3. **Check the corpus.** Chronos: the paper's Table 3; Chronos-2: Table 6; TimesFM: Wikipedia, Google
   Trends, M4; TimeGPT: undisclosed. If your data, or a public version of it, is listed, say so.
4. **Check the dates.** A model released before your holdout began cannot have seen it.
5. **Report the interval too**, and score its coverage (Week 8).
6. **For TimeGPT:** your own key, in a Colab secret — never in the notebook you submit.

# Wrapping up

## Eight ways to get this wrong {.tiny}

| Trap | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A test window inside the pretraining corpus | Results that look too good | Corpus lists, release dates, data newer than the model |
| Choosing the foundation model on the test | An optimistic winner | Validation windows, then one test |
| A model used outside its frequencies | Lag-Llama on monthly data | Check what it was trained on; fine-tune or choose another |
| Covariates whose future is not known | A forecast that cannot be made in practice | Only truly known covariates, or forecast them first |
| Fine-tuning taken as an improvement | Sometimes it is worse | Score it like any candidate |
| An API key in a notebook | A leaked key, a spent quota | Environment variable or Colab secret |
| Company data sent to an API | A privacy problem | Ask first; an open model runs locally |
| "Foundation" read as "better" | Losing to ARIMA on your series | One more candidate on the rolling origin |

## What this lecture is, in one slide {.smaller}

- A **foundation model** is a model trained once on large, diverse data and used on many tasks — here,
  any series, zero-shot. Almost always a **transformer**: tokens, positional encoding, attention.
- **Pretraining → transfer → fine-tuning**, done in miniature with N-BEATS on M3, works — and is limited
  by one horizon, one frequency, one corpus. The real models fix those with generation, patches and
  billions of observations.
- **TimeGPT** (API, conformal intervals, covariates), **Lag-Llama** (open, Student-$t$, sub-daily only),
  **Chronos** (a language model on binned values), **Moirai** (any-variate, mixture output), **TimesFM**
  (point forecasts, long output patches) differ in architecture, output, covariates and access.
- On our four stores they forecast well with no fitting; how they compare with ARIMA, and with each
  other, is a question for **your** data and **your** holdout — never settled by a benchmark table.
